units.text: INT. HUSBAND - CONTINUOUS
No, my lord.
units.name: PHIPPS

units.text: I am not quite sure. For the future a more trivial buttonhole, Phipps, on Thursday evenings.
units.name: LORD GORING

units.text: I will speak to the florist, my lord. She has had a loss in her family lately, which perhaps accounts for the lack of triviality your lordship complains of in the buttonhole.
units.name: PHIPPS

units.text: Extraordinary thing about the lower classes in England—they are always losing their relations.
units.name: LORD GORING

units.text: Yes, my lord! They are extremely fortunate in that respect.
units.name: PHIPPS

units.text: Turns round and looks at him .
PHIPPS remains impassive .
Hum! Any letters, Phipps?
units.name: LORD GORING

units.text: Three, my lord.
units.name: PHIPPS

units.text: Hands letters on a salver .
Takes letters .
Want my cab round in twenty minutes.
units.name: LORD GORING

units.text: Yes, my lord.
units.name: PHIPPS

units.text: Goes towards door .
Holds up letter in pink envelope .
Ahem! Phipps, when did this letter arrive?
units.name: LORD GORING

units.text: It was brought by hand just after your lordship went to the club.
units.name: PHIPPS

units.text: That will do.
units.name: LORD GORING

units.text: Exit PHIPPS.
Lady Chiltern’s handwriting on Lady Chiltern’s pink notepaper. That is rather curious. I thought Robert was to write. Wonder what Lady Chiltern has got to say to me?
units.name: LORD GORING

units.text: Sits at bureau and opens letter , and reads it .
‘I want you. I trust you. I am coming to you. Gertrude.’
units.name: LORD GORING

units.text: Puts down the letter with a puzzled look .
Then takes it up , and reads it again slowly .
‘I want you. I trust you. I am coming to you.’ So she has found out everything! Poor woman! Poor woman!
units.name: LORD GORING

units.text: Pulls out watch and looks at it .

But what an hour to call! Ten o’clock! I shall have to give up going to the Berkshires. However, it is always nice to be expected, and not to arrive. I am not expected at the Bachelors’, so I shall certainly go there. Well, I will make her stand by her husband. That is the only thing for her to do. That is the only thing for any woman to do. It is the growth of the moral sense in women that makes marriage such a hopeless, one-sided institution. Ten o’clock. She should be here soon. I must tell Phipps I am not in to any one else.
units.name: LORD GORING

units.text: Goes towards bell .
Enter PHIPPS.
Lord Caversham.
units.name: PHIPPS

units.text: Oh, why will parents always appear at the wrong time? Some extraordinary mistake in nature, I suppose.
units.name: LORD GORING

units.text: Enter LORD CAVERSHAM.
Delighted to see you, my dear father.
units.name: LORD GORING

units.text: Goes to meet him .
Take my cloak off.
units.name: LORD CAVERSHAM

units.text: Is it worth while, father?
units.name: LORD GORING

units.text: Of course it is worth while, sir. Which is the most comfortable chair?
units.name: LORD CAVERSHAM

units.text: This one, father. It is the chair I use myself, when I have visitors.
units.name: LORD GORING

units.text: Thank ye. No draught, I hope, in this room?
units.name: LORD CAVERSHAM

units.text: No, father.
units.name: LORD GORING

units.text: Sitting down .
Glad to hear it. Can’t stand draughts. No draughts at home.
units.name: LORD CAVERSHAM

units.text: Good many breezes, father.
units.name: LORD GORING

units.text: Eh? Eh? Don’t understand what you mean. Want to have a serious conversation with you, sir.
units.name: LORD CAVERSHAM

units.text: My dear father! At this hour?
units.name: LORD GORING

units.text: Well, sir, it is only ten o’clock. What is your objection to the hour? I think the hour is an admirable hour!
units.name: LORD CAVERSHAM

units.text: Well, the fact is, father, this is not my day for talking seriously. I am very sorry, but it is not my day.
units.name: LORD GORING
